answers.T4_traffic:
For N = 256, the naive dot products contain Q = N(N-1)(N+1)/6 = 2796160 multiply-adds; two Float64 loads per term give 16Q = 44738560 modeled bytes 
    and 21.806 GB/s when divided by the measured time 0.002052 s. Left-looking took 0.000377 s (a naive/left time ratio of 5.441), 
    and its contiguous i-loop enables SIMD, prefetching and reuse of the active column. Its update operands involve two loads 
    and one store per element without reuse, but caches can avoid much of this DRAM traffic, so operand counts alone do not predict bandwidth.     The modeled rate is 1.744x the measured STREAM bandwidth of 12.501 GB/s; differences reflect the model assumptions and cache 
    reuse rather than literal DRAM traffic.
answers.T1_dependencies:
In the row-by-row baseline, each row uses previously computed entries of L, so arbitrary rows cannot be factored independently. 
    After column j is factored and scaled in the right-looking form, each task updates separate trailing columns using the completed column j, 
    avoiding conflicting writes. The @sync barrier ensures all these updates finish before the next pivot is read.
answers.T1_scaling:
At N = 256, the best speed-up was 1.000x at p = 1 task groups; at p = 12, speed-up was 0.036x and efficiency was 0.003. 
    The constrained Amdahl fit gave an effective serial fraction f = 1.0000 with speed-up RMSE 0.8686. 
    Sequential column factorization/scaling, a barrier after each trailing update, task scheduling, 
    and memory bandwidth limit scaling and can even cause a slowdown, so this fitted fraction is not a direct measurement of purely serial work.
answers.T4_cache:
Detected L2 cache-domain capacities are 1310720, 2097152 bytes; using the smallest domain, 1310720 bytes, 
    three Float64 tiles fit when nb <= 233, and the largest fitting candidate is nb = 128. The measured BEST_NB = 256 does not fit this capacity model. This is a capacity estimate, 
    not a guarantee of residency: shared L2 caches, concurrent tasks and other working data reduce usable space. 
    Small tiles improve cache fit but increase scheduling overhead, so the measured optimum need not be the largest fitting tile.
answers.T5_gap:
At N = 256, LAPACK reached 31.08 GFlop/s, while our best hand-written loop (left) reached 48.7% of that, and tiled_blas (nb = 256) reached 94.5%. 
    Vendor BLAS-3 kernels block for registers, L1 and L2, pack panels into contiguous buffers so the micro-kernel streams unit-stride data, use fully 
    unrolled SIMD micro-kernels with FMA on every cycle (2 FP64 lanes per 128-bit NEON register on this Neoverse-N1), and prefetch the next panel. 
    Our loops do far fewer flops per byte loaded and leave the FMA units idle while waiting on memory.
answers.T2_barriers:
Two @sync barriers wait after TRSM and after UPDATE.
   A DAG scheduler could start each update once its inputs are ready, and the next POTRF once its diagonal tile is fully updated.
answers.T5_oversubscription:
Julia runs 12 threads and OpenBLAS can run 12 threads, but the machine has only 12 logical cores. If every tile task called a multi-threaded BLAS kernel, 
    up to 12 x 12 threads would compete for the cores, causing context switches and cache thrashing. cholesky_tiled_blas! sets BLAS.set_num_threads(1) 
    during the parallel part and restores the previous value in a finally block, so parallelism comes only from the tile tasks. LAPACK went from 0.181 ms 
    (1 BLAS thread) to 1.055 ms (12 BLAS threads).
answers.T3_tradeoff:
Float32 factorization was 1.224 times faster than Float64.
    Backward error increased from 2.26e-16 to 1.41e-7,
    corresponding to approximately 8.8 digits lost.
    Forward error increased from 3.18e-14 to 1.29e-5,
    corresponding to approximately 8.6 digits lost.
    Float32 was faster but less accurate. Forward error also
    depends on the conditioning of the matrix.
answers.T3_ir:
Iterative refinement computes residuals in Float64, solves
    for corrections using the existing Float32 Cholesky factors,
    and updates the solution in Float64. Accurate residuals allow
    it to recover accuracy close to Float64 precision.

    In our experiment, two corrections achieved backward error
    4.52e-16, below the requested tolerance. However, mixed precision
    took 0.009514 s versus 0.0006824 s for Float64: about 13.9 times
    slower, because the additional work outweighed the faster factorization.

    Convergence generally requires kappa(A)*eps(Float32) sufficiently
    smaller than 1. If A is too ill-conditioned, inaccurate correction
    solves can cause stagnation or failure to converge.
answers.T2_granularity:
Small tiles incur scheduling overhead; large tiles reduce available parallelism.
    For N = 256, nb = 256 was fastest (~0.6 ms), but spawned no tasks.
    Confirm the choice with QUICK = false.
